title: Maximum likelihood requires noise that degrades sample quality
description: The paper states that adding noise to model distributions to make maximum likelihood approaches work degrades the quality of samples and makes them blurry, citing evidence that optimal noise levels for likelihood are very high.

verdict.reasoning: Paper 3 ("Normalizing Flows are Capable Generative Models") directly solves the gap. It acknowledges that noise augmentation is necessary for MLE-based normalizing flows, and that this noise indeed produces blurry/noisy samples. But it shows this degradation can be fully overcome with a simple, principled solution: use Gaussian noise (not uniform) and apply a training-free score-based denoising step (Tweedie's formula) at generation time. The result is state-of-the-art FID scores comparable to diffusion models on ImageNet and AFHQ — directly disproving the claim that MLE-required noise inevitably degrades sample quality into blurriness. Paper 1 ("Data Mollification") provides partial corroboration by showing that annealing noise schedules can improve sample quality even without a denoising step, though it still reverts to clean training where manifold overfitting can occur. Paper 2 ("Exponential Tilting") is a workaround (post-hoc EBM correction) that does not address the core claim. Taken together, the evidence shows the gap has been resolved for an important class of MLE-based models (normalizing flows on images), with a clear recipe that directly addresses the noise-degradation tension.

paper.title: One-Line-of-Code Data Mollification Improves Optimization of Likelihood-based Generative Models
paper.abstract: Generative Models (GMs) have attracted considerable attention due to their tremendous success in various domains, such as computer vision where they are capable to generate impressive realistic-looking images. Likelihood-based GMs are attractive due to the possibility to generate new data by a single model evaluation. However, they typically achieve lower sample quality compared to state-of-the-art score-based diffusion models (DMs). This paper provides a significant step in the direction of addressing this limitation. The idea is to borrow one of the strengths of score-based DMs, which is the ability to perform accurate density estimation in low-density regions and to address manifold overfitting by means of data mollification. We connect data mollification through the addition of Gaussian noise to Gaussian homotopy, which is a well-known technique to improve optimization. Data mollification can be implemented by adding one line of code in the optimization loop, and we demonstrate that this provides a boost in generation quality of likelihood-based GMs, without computational overheads. We report results on image data sets with popular likelihood-based GMs, including variants of variational autoencoders and normalizing flows, showing large improvements in FID score.

assessments.contribution_summary: This paper proposes data mollification (adding Gaussian noise with an annealing schedule) to improve optimization of likelihood-based generative models like VAEs and normalizing flows. The key idea is to start with heavily noise-corrupted data (easy to model) and gradually reduce the noise level during training, acting as a continuation method. The paper shows that this approach consistently improves sample quality (measured by FID scores) across multiple image datasets and model architectures, contrary to the claim that noise necessarily degrades sample quality in maximum likelihood approaches.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper does not fully resolve the gap because: (1) It still relies on training with clean data (zero noise) in the second half of optimization, where manifold overfitting can still occur — the paper acknowledges that "when removing the last bit of perturbation we fall back to the case where we experience manifold overfitting" and relies on stochasticity/gradient clipping to avoid degenerate solutions. (2) The improvements in FID score, while substantial, are still far from state-of-the-art diffusion models — the paper states "we are far from closing the gap with DMs in achieving competing FID score." (3) The paper does not address the fundamental tension that maximum likelihood objectives may inherently require noise for well-behaved density estimation in high dimensions, and the optimal noise level for likelihood may still be high; instead it shows that annealing noise as an optimization trick helps, but the final model still trains without noise.
evidence_snippets: When removing the last bit of perturbation we fall back to the case where we experience manifold overfitting. However, when we operate in a stochastic setting, which is the typical scenario for the GMs considered here, we avoid ending up in solutions for which the density is degenerate and with support which is exactly the data manifold.
the improvements in FID score indicate that the performance boost is generally substantial, but still far from being comparable with state-of-the-art DMs.
While we are far from closing the gap with DMs in achieving competing FID score, we are confident that this work will serve as the basis for future works on performance improvements

paper.title: Exponential Tilting of Generative Models: Improving Sample Quality by Training and Sampling from Latent Energy
paper.abstract: In this paper, we present a general method that can improve the sample quality of pre-trained likelihood based generative models. Our method constructs an energy function on the latent variable space that yields an energy function on samples produced by the pre-trained generative model. The energy based model is efficiently trained by maximizing the data likelihood, and after training, new samples in the latent space are generated from the energy based model and passed through the generator to producing samples in observation space. We show that using our proposed method, we can greatly improve the sample quality of popular likelihood based generative models, such as normalizing flows and VAEs, with very little computational overhead.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper proposes training an energy-based model (EBM) on the latent space of pre-trained likelihood-based generative models (normalizing flows, VAEs). The EBM is trained by maximum likelihood and used to re-weight latent variables, producing sharper samples from the same generator. This improves sample quality post-hoc without modifying the base model's training.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper does not address the gap's core claim that maximum likelihood estimation inherently requires adding noise to distributions, which degrades sample quality and causes blurriness. The paper's approach still uses maximum likelihood (to train the EBM) and does not propose an alternative to the noise-adding requirement of MLE. It works around the problem by adding a post-hoc correction (EBM sampling) rather than solving the fundamental limitation of MLE itself. The question of whether maximum likelihood can be made to work without degrading noise remains entirely open.
evidence_snippets: This paper aims at a slightly different task: we want to improve the sample quality of an existing generative model through a better sampling procedure.

We show that using our proposed method, we can greatly improve the sample quality of popular likelihood based generative models, such as normalizing flows and VAEs, with very little computational overhead.
The EBM can be trained by the maximum likelihood principle, namely minimizing the negative log likelihood

paper.title: Normalizing Flows are Capable Generative Models
paper.abstract: Normalizing Flows (NFs) are likelihood-based models for continuous inputs. They have demonstrated promising results on both density estimation and generative modeling tasks, but have received relatively little attention in recent years. In this work, we demonstrate that NFs are more powerful than previously believed. We present TarFlow: a simple and scalable architecture that enables highly performant NF models. TarFlow can be thought of as a Transformer-based variant of Masked Autoregressive Flows (MAFs): it consists of a stack of autoregressive Transformer blocks on image patches, alternating the autoregression direction between layers. TarFlow is straightforward to train end-to-end, and capable of directly modeling and generating pixels. We also propose three key techniques to improve sample quality: Gaussian noise augmentation during training, a post training denoising procedure, and an effective guidance method for both class-conditional and unconditional settings. Putting these together, TarFlow sets new state-of-the-art results on likelihood estimation for images, beating the previous best methods by a large margin, and generates samples with quality and diversity comparable to diffusion models, for the first time with a stand-alone NF model. We make our code available at https://github.com/apple/ml-tarflow.

assessments.contribution_summary: This paper directly addresses the gap that maximum likelihood approaches require adding noise which degrades sample quality. The authors identify that for Normalizing Flows, the standard dequantization uniform noise is insufficient for good generation, and propose using Gaussian noise augmentation during training combined with a post-training score-based denoising procedure (via Tweedie's formula) to remove the noise from generated samples. They demonstrate that this combination — moderate Gaussian noise + denoising — yields state-of-the-art sample quality (FID comparable to diffusion models) on ImageNet and AFHQ, directly solving the noise-degradation problem.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper fully addresses the gap for the specific case of Normalizing Flows on image data. It shows that the noise-required-by-MLE problem can be solved by (a) using Gaussian rather than uniform noise, and (b) applying a post-hoc denoising step. The gap as stated ("maximum likelihood requires noise that degrades sample quality") is directly solved by this work — the paper demonstrates that with the right noise type and a denoising procedure, MLE-based models can produce high-quality samples without blurriness. No significant part of the gap remains open for this model class.
evidence_snippets: For better perceptual quality during sampling, however, we show that it is critical to set $p_{\epsilon}(\cdot)$ as a Gaussian distribution $\mathcal{N}(\cdot; 0, \sigma^2 \mathrm{I})$ whose magnitude $\sigma$ is small but larger than that of the pixel quantization bin size.

Training with noise augmentation introduces an additional challenge: models trained on the noisy distribution $q(y)$ naturally generate outputs that mimic noisy training examples, rather than clean ones. This results in samples that are less visually appealing. As a remedy, we propose a straightforward training-free technique that effectively denoises the generated samples, by drawing inspiration from score-based generative models.

Denoising successfully cleans up the noisy raw samples, and as a result the best visual quality occurs at a moderate (but still relatively small) amount of noise. This verifies the necessity of our proposed sampling procedure, whereas the combination of noise augmented training and the score based denoising step work organically together to produce the best generative capability.
